headline: GOOG surged nearly 4% last night on fresh investor optimism, but PLS.AX took a nasty 4.5% hit today as lithium sentiment stays sour.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara had a rough session today, dropping 4.5% to $6.14. The big news is that Morgan Stanley has ceased to be a substantial holder — meaning the investment bank sold down its stake below the 5% disclosure threshold. When a major institutional investor exits a position like that, it often drags the price down as the market reads it as a loss of confidence. Lithium prices remain depressed globally, and sentiment on the sector is still firmly negative.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: GOOG jumped nearly 4% last night to USD $369.43, its best single-session move in a while. Alphabet held an investor presentation in June 2026, and there's growing buzz around its AI search and cloud revenue growth prospects. The market is rewarding Google for staying competitive in the AI race — your position is now up 27.8% overall.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: The AI ETF dropped 2.4% today to $18.37, which is a bit ironic given GOOG's strong night. The ASX-listed ETF moves on the previous US session and broader ASX sentiment, and today's local market was soft across the board. The ETF holds a basket of global AI stocks, so it doesn't always move in lockstep with any single name like Google.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG dipped about 1% today to $75.86. As a diversified fund holding Australian and international shares, it broadly followed the softer ASX session today. No specific catalyst — just general market drift. You're still slightly in the green overall (+0.64%).

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE slipped 0.64% today to $92.90. Emerging markets have been under mild pressure with the Aussie dollar softening slightly against the USD, which can affect the local-currency value of these offshore holdings. Marginally underwater on this position (-1%).

movers.name: BetaShares Global Energy Companies ETF
movers.note: FUEL edged up 0.8% today to $8.77, a small bright spot. However, crude oil fell sharply last night — down 3.8% to USD $92.34 — so watch this space. The ETF tracks global energy companies, and if oil keeps sliding, expect some pressure on FUEL in coming sessions. Still up 3.7% overall from your entry.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS dipped 0.45% today to $520.21. This ETF mirrors the US total sharemarket, so today's local move reflects the previous US session and any currency drag. The S&P 500 was up slightly last night, so the dip here is likely AUD/USD noise at the margins. Still up 0.87% overall.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two crept up 0.58% last night to USD $217.06. No major fundamental news — the biggest headline was fans breaking into Rockstar Games' office, which is more of a curiosity than a market mover. The stock remains down 6.4% from your entry cost. GTA 6 hype keeps a floor under the price, but there's no near-term catalyst to push it higher.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft was essentially flat last night, down just $0.17 to $427.17. No major news out — Q1 earnings already digested. Microsoft's AI Chief Mustafa Suleyman made headlines saying his team is more worried about Anthropic than Google or Meta in the AI race, which suggests internal confidence in Microsoft's position. Still down 3.6% overall from your entry.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX — Morgan Stanley exits, stock down 4.5%
watch_today.detail: Morgan Stanley dropped below the 5% substantial holder threshold in Pilbara Minerals today, meaning they've been selling. Combined with persistently weak lithium prices globally, PLS fell 4.5% to $6.14 and is now down 8.9% from your entry. It's painful, but selling now locks in the loss. Hold unless your conviction in the lithium recovery thesis has changed — no new fundamental collapse today, just an institutional exit.

watch_today.title: GOOG — Big 4% jump last night, momentum building
watch_today.detail: Alphabet surged nearly 4% last night to USD $369.43 after a June investor presentation reinforced confidence in Google's AI and cloud growth story. Your position is now up 27.8% overall. No need to chase — just enjoy the ride. If the US market opens strong tonight (11:30 PM AEST), GOOG could extend the move.

watch_today.title: Oil down 3.8% last night — watch FUEL.AX this week
watch_today.detail: Crude oil (WTI) dropped sharply last night from $96 to $92.34 — a fall of about 3.8%. FUEL.AX actually ticked up 0.8% today, but that's likely a lag effect. If oil stays under pressure, FUEL will feel it within a session or two. Keep an eye on oil prices this week before adding to this position.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX — AI ETF dips 2.4% despite strong GOOG night
watch_today.detail: The Global X AI ETF fell 2.4% today to $18.37, now down 3.5% from your entry. The ASX-listed ETF tracks last night's US AI names, so it should get a boost tomorrow when it catches up to GOOG's strong session. Hold — no reason to sell ahead of what should be a positive open for AI stocks tomorrow.

watch_today.title: US AI regulation — new laws could reshape Google & Microsoft
watch_today.detail: The US House released a draft bill today to regulate AI that would override state-level AI laws and create a federal framework. Separately, Trump's administration is moving to 'pre-check' AI models from OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic before launch. This adds regulatory uncertainty for GOOG and MSFT — not an immediate threat, but worth watching as the bill moves through Congress.

watch_today.title: RBA — rate hikes back on the table, two more years of pain warned
watch_today.detail: The RBA's Governor Bullock flagged today that inflation is likely to rise further in the near term, and multiple outlets are warning of two more years of economic pain. The AFR also linked the AI boom to contributing to the RBA's recent U-turn on rates. Higher rates for longer means tighter conditions for Aussie households and could weigh on local ETFs like VDHG. Keep this in mind if you're considering adding to ASX positions.

markets.summary: Last night on Wall Street, the S&P 500 edged up 0.47% and the NASDAQ gained 0.1% — a quiet, slightly positive session. The big story was crude oil tumbling 3.8% to USD $92.34, which could hurt energy stocks this week. Gold jumped 1.56% to a very lofty USD $4,505, showing investors are still parking money in safe havens. The Aussie dollar softened slightly, down 0.45% to about 71.4 US cents. ASX 200 data wasn't available for today's close.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Slight gain last night — market holding up despite macro uncertainty.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Essentially flat last night, GOOG's big night didn't drag the whole index higher.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Today's ASX 200 close data unavailable — using previous close as reference.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Sharp drop last night — could weigh on FUEL.AX in coming sessions.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold at very elevated levels — investors still seeking safety.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: Aussie dollar softened slightly — mild headwind for unhedged overseas holdings.

politics.summary: It's a big day in Canberra — Labor's budget bills are stuck in the Senate, the RBA is warning of more pain ahead, and a new journalism levy is drawing fire from Meta. Plenty happening that affects your hip pocket.

stories.title: RBA warns inflation to rise further — two more years of economic pain ahead
stories.why_it_matters: RBA Governor Michele Bullock said today that inflation is likely to rise further in the near term, dashing hopes of quick rate relief. Multiple media outlets are reporting the bank is warning Australians to brace for up to two more years of economic pain. The AFR also linked the unexpected AI productivity boom as one factor that contributed to the RBA's recent U-turn on rate policy — basically, stronger-than-expected economic activity made the bank reconsider cutting rates. For homeowners or anyone with debt, this is bad news: rates aren't coming down anytime soon.

stories.title: Coalition and Greens block Labor's major budget bills in Senate
stories.why_it_matters: Labor's key budget legislation is stuck in limbo after both the Coalition and the Greens refused to support it in the Senate. This is a significant political setback for the Albanese government — without Senate support, the budget measures (including spending commitments and potential tax changes) can't pass into law. It creates uncertainty about Australia's fiscal direction, which matters for bond markets and government spending flowing through the economy. Expect more horse-trading in Parliament over coming weeks.

stories.title: Albanese government's new tax laws slammed as 'constitutionally invalid'
stories.why_it_matters: Sky News host Sharri Markson is reporting that legal experts believe Labor's new tax legislation may be constitutionally invalid. While the specific legal argument wasn't fully detailed, this adds another layer of uncertainty to the government's budget agenda — on top of the Senate blockage. If the legislation faces a High Court challenge, key revenue and spending measures could be tied up in legal proceedings for months or years. Worth watching if you have any exposure to sectors targeted by the new tax laws.

stories.title: Meta calls Albanese journalism levy 'indefensible'
stories.why_it_matters: Meta (Facebook's parent company) has hit out hard at Labor's proposed journalism levy — a plan to make big tech platforms like Facebook pay Australian news publishers for their content. Meta called the plan 'indefensible' and is pushing back publicly. This is a rematch of the 2021 News Media Bargaining Code fight where Meta briefly blocked Australian news on Facebook. If Meta digs in again, it could become a diplomatic and regulatory flashpoint — and a headwind for Meta's Australian operations. Your GOOG holding could also be indirectly affected if similar rules are expanded to Google.

ai.summary: US AI regulation is the big story today — both a new presidential order and a House draft bill are moving to put guardrails on how the big AI labs release models. Meanwhile, Microsoft's AI chief is naming Anthropic as the real threat, and a benchmark test showed GPT-5.5 stomping the competition.

stories.title: Trump signs order requiring pre-approval of AI models before launch
stories.why_it_matters: Trump's administration is now requiring that AI models from OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic go through a government pre-check process before they can be publicly launched. Think of it like a product safety inspection, but for AI. Separately, the US House released a draft bill that would create a single federal AI rulebook, overriding the patchwork of different state laws. For companies like Google (your GOOG holding) and Microsoft (MSFT), this adds a compliance layer — but it also locks out smaller competitors who can't afford the regulatory process, which could actually entrench the big players' advantages.

stories.title: Microsoft AI chief says Anthropic is the competitor keeping him up at night
stories.why_it_matters: Mustafa Suleyman, the CEO of Microsoft AI, said publicly that his team is 'more concerned' about Anthropic (the company behind the Claude chatbot) than about Google, Meta, or OpenAI. He called Anthropic the toughest competitor in the enterprise AI space — meaning businesses using AI tools at work. This is an interesting admission that Microsoft sees Claude as a genuine threat to its own Copilot AI products. For MSFT holders, it suggests the competition isn't over and Microsoft will need to keep investing heavily to stay ahead.

stories.title: GPT-5.5 dominates benchmark test — Gemini (Google) refused to even attempt it
stories.why_it_matters: In a competitive $1,500 'LLM hacking test' (a benchmark that pits AI models against each other on complex tasks), OpenAI's GPT-5.5 came out on top. More embarrassingly for Google, its Gemini model reportedly refused to even attempt the test — likely due to safety guardrails that made it too cautious. This kind of benchmark matters because enterprise customers use them to decide which AI tools to adopt. It's a small reputational ding for Google's AI division, even as the broader Alphabet business is performing well.

stories.title: House draft bill would create one national AI rulebook, killing state laws
stories.why_it_matters: US House lawmakers released a draft AI regulation bill today that would set one federal standard for AI across all 50 states, overriding laws that states like California have been building. This is significant because it would simplify (and arguably loosen) the regulatory environment for big AI companies — they'd deal with one regulator instead of 50. For Google and Microsoft, a single federal framework is generally preferable to a state-by-state patchwork. The bill is still in draft form and faces a long road through Congress.

sport.summary: Big NRL Round 14 news today: Manly beat the Rabbits 28-14 last night in a game marred by a controversial 'sticky spray' no-call, and there's some interesting club drama heading into the weekend's fixtures. On the AFL front, the football world is rallying around Adelaide captain Jordan Dawson.

stories.title: Manly 28 def. Rabbitohs 14 — sticky spray controversy steals headlines
stories.why_it_matters: Manly Sea Eagles defeated South Sydney Rabbitohs 28-14 at 4 Pines Park in the first game of Round 14. The post-match discussion is dominated by a controversial referee decision involving 'sticky spray' — the foam referees use to mark penalty positions — that went against the Bunnies at a critical moment. Manly's resurgence under Kieran Foran continues, with the veteran halfback playing a key role again. Souths will be fuming about the call. Manly also dealt with an injury scare during the game but the full extent isn't yet confirmed.

stories.title: Manly gun sin-binned, teammate 'in strife' for chicken wing tackle
stories.why_it_matters: Adding to Manly's disciplinary headaches from Thursday night's game, one of their key players was sin-binned during the match, and a teammate is reportedly facing scrutiny from the match review committee for a chicken wing tackle — an illegal move that bends the arm behind an opponent's back. Depending on the review outcome, Manly could be without that player for upcoming games, which would be a blow to their momentum.

stories.title: Tigers star says 'I'll never be loyal to a club' — Benji Marshall at the centre
stories.why_it_matters: A Wests Tigers player has made a shocking public declaration that he will 'never be loyal to a club,' directly implicating coach Benji Marshall in his future decision. It's a bold statement that suggests some unrest in the Tigers camp ahead of their Sunday clash against the Panthers. With the Tigers already struggling for form, this kind of public drama is the last thing Benji needs. The player's contract situation and relationship with Marshall will be a major storyline this week.

stories.title: AFL world rallies around 'superhuman' Adelaide captain Jordan Dawson
stories.why_it_matters: The AFL world is rallying around Adelaide Crows captain Jordan Dawson, with 7NEWS describing an emotional outpouring of support for him. Dawson has been praised as 'superhuman' — though the specific circumstances that prompted this wave of support weren't detailed in the available report. It appears to be a significant personal or on-field moment for the Crows captain that has resonated strongly across the football community heading into Round 13 of the AFL season.
